# Meaning as Generation: Producing and Growing Meaning {#sec-ch-meaning-as-generation}

Meaning is not only read; it is made and grown. A space of meanings that can be read only is a catalogue, and the same space that can also be written to is a way to produce what has not been said: a sentence that fits, an image of a dog that no one photographed, a molecule, a hypothesis in a field where nobody has looked. Chomsky's generative grammar made production the test of a theory of language [@chomsky1957syntactic; @chomsky1965aspects], and Wittgenstein's use includes saying new things with old words [@wittgenstein1953philosophical]. The question of this chapter is what a latent space does when it is used to make and not to read: how a point becomes an object, what happens when the point lies beyond the data, where new regions might be, and what separates a plausible object from a true or a useful one.

The scope is production and growth. Travel between points that the data already hold is the chapter on paths (@sec-ch-meaning-as-path), and its geometry (curves, metrics, geodesics) is taken from there; whether a product is true is the chapter on truth (@sec-ch-meaning-and-truth), which takes from here the contrast between plausible and true; the sense that a decoder gives to a point depends on its context (@sec-ch-meaning-in-context); and a combination of known parts into a new whole is the chapter on composition (@sec-ch-meaning-as-composition).

*Goals and expectations (proposed, to be confirmed by the author before any experiment). A first search for the literature was made on 2026-11-22 (author's request) and the sources it found are in `references/`; they were read at the level of the abstract and the passages quoted below, and are to be read before the chapter is written. One source that the author knows, on how far the output of a model recombines the ideas discussed in the prompt, has not been identified yet.*

*Goal 1, decoding a point into an object.* The expectation is that a latent variable model that is given a density over its space can draw a new point and say how likely a point is, which a map from data to vectors cannot, and that the decoder gives each point an object (@sec-giving-space-density-latent). The run is the variational autoencoder on the digits of the repository, with samples from the prior.

*Goal 2, beyond the data.* Travel over unknown territory is where nothing has fixed a metric or says whether a point means anything. The distinction between interpolating among known ideas and extrapolating beyond them has a further difficulty in a space of many dimensions: Balestriero, Pesenti and LeCun show that on any dataset of more than about a hundred dimensions a new sample almost surely falls outside the convex hull of the data, so that interpolation in the strict sense almost never happens and the usual definition is not an indicator of how well a model generalizes [@balestriero2021learning; @bonnassegahot2022interpolation]. The question is therefore not whether a decoded point is an interpolation or an extrapolation, which in high dimension is nearly always the second, but how far it is from the data, in which directions, and in what measure of plausibility. The expectation is that the plausibility of a decoded point falls with its distance from the data, and that the fall is steeper for a model with a sharper density; the run decodes points at growing distances from the encoded digits and measures plausibility with a classifier (@sec-gen-beyond-data).

*Goal 3, the map stops (Where the Map Stops).* The expectation is that the objectives that learn a map from data to vectors cannot draw a new point or score one, and that the generative objectives can, at the price of normalization or of a game (@sec-where-map-stops, @sec-reconciling-two-families).

*Goal 4, plausible is not true.* A model that produces what is typical produces the typical error; the expectation and the test are those of the chapter on truth (@sec-plausible-true).

*Goal 4b, what is novel in what a model produces.* The expectation is that on the surface (word sequences) a model's text is mostly new at the level of whole sentences and structure and copies at the level of short strings, and sometimes long passages [@mccoy2023raven; @merrill2024ngram]; that at the level of ideas LLM-generated research ideas are judged more novel than human ones by blind expert reviewers and weaker in feasibility [@si2024novel], while a considerable share is paraphrase of existing work without acknowledgement [@gupta2025glitters]; that novelty is better measured as the frontier of originality and quality, where scale and post-training raise it and prompting and in-context examples have a smaller effect [@padmakumar2025novelty]; and that diffusion models move from memorizing the training set to generalizing through an inductive bias toward geometry-adaptive harmonic representations [@kadkhodaie2024generalization]. The creativity surveys give the frame of exploratory and transformational creativity [@franceschelli2024creativityml; @franceschelli2023creativityllm]. The run, if any, measures the distance of generated items to their nearest training item in a latent space, and does not decide between recombination and invention.

*Goal 5, where are the new regions? (an idea).* If the space of the published literature is embedded, regions that are sparse between dense ones are candidates for a new topic, as in literature-based discovery, where a link between two literatures that do not cite each other is a hypothesis. The expectation is that such gaps contain future work more often than random gaps; the run needs a corpus with dates, and the sources are Swanson's literature-based discovery, where two literatures that do not cite each other are linked through arguments that they share: a set of articles showing that dietary fish oils change the blood and vessels, and another showing that such changes might benefit patients with Raynaud's syndrome, had no article in common and had never been cited together, and the first clinical trial of the effect was reported by others two years after the analysis [@swanson1990medical, p. 29]. Swanson describes the process as one of "excising and recombining ideas from scientific literatures in order to generate new ideas", close to a natural-selection model of science whose variability lies in the recombination of ideas (p. 31), and says that his search strategy "is neither a recipe nor an algorithm" and depends on the knowledge and ingenuity of the searcher (p. 31), and the finding that word embeddings of three million materials-science abstracts recommend materials for a function several years before their discovery [@tshitoyan2019unsupervised] (@sec-gen-new-regions).

## What the Philosophies Say About Making Meaning {#sec-gen-philosophy}
*Plan (about 3 pages). Chomsky's generative grammar and the distinction between competence and performance [@chomsky1957syntactic; @chomsky1965aspects; @chomsky1986knowledge]; Wittgenstein on use and on the rule that is followed [@wittgenstein1953philosophical]; Ramsey on meaning by consequences [@ramsey1927facts]; and creativity as exploring a conceptual space or transforming it (Boden, in the account of the surveys [@franceschelli2024creativityml; @franceschelli2023creativityllm]; Boden's own book is not in the collection and is to be read before it is quoted). Gärdenfors's quality spaces give the first a geometry, a region to explore, and the second a change of the space itself. For each: what making meaning would be, what a latent space carries of it, and where it stops.*

## Beyond the Data {#sec-gen-beyond-data}
*Plan (about 3 pages). Goal 2. Points decoded at growing distance from the data, their plausibility, and the null of random latent points; the relation to the geometry the decoder induces (the chapter on paths), to the density the model assigns, and to the manifold hypothesis of the appendix.*

## Where Are the New Regions? {#sec-gen-new-regions}
*Plan (about 2 pages; an idea). Goal 5. A map of a corpus with dates, the sparse regions between dense ones, and the check of whether later work falls in them more often than in random gaps. Truth directions, from the chapter on truth, could steer toward a region and are not assumed to.*


<!-- salvaged from embedding-technologies-stubs/generative_spaces.qmd, section sec-fork-map-distribution -->
## The Fork: A Map or a Distribution? {#sec-fork-map-distribution}
*The objectives of @sec-ch-meaning-as-likeness learn a map from data to vectors; none of them can draw a new point or say how likely a point is. A model that defines a distribution over the data can do both, and its hidden variables are what the literature calls the latent space. Two questions classify every objective of the two chapters: where is the error measured (in the data, among sampled candidates, in the code), and is there a distribution over the data. Terminology: where the literature has settled on one word for a context, the book uses it (latent variable, latent diffusion against word embedding).*

<!-- salvaged from embedding-technologies-stubs/generative_spaces.qmd, section sec-giving-space-density-latent -->
## Giving the Space a Density: Latent Variable Models and the VAE {#sec-giving-space-density-latent}
*The hidden-cause view (factor analysis, the "latent" of LSA, EM). The evidence lower bound as a reconstruction term plus a prior term, read against the autoencoder of @sec-ch-meaning-as-likeness: the same decoder with a prior added. What the prior buys (sampling, smoothness) and what it costs (posterior collapse, the cousin of the dimensional collapse of @sec-ch-meaning-as-likeness; holes between the codes). Identifiability: the standard prior is rotation-symmetric, so the invertible-matrix freedom of @sec-ch-meaning-as-likeness survives as a rotation freedom, and disentanglement is not free.*

*Note: automatic differentiation in depth (the dissolved chapter on the anatomy of embedding spaces (kept in `embedding-technologies-stubs/`) derives the backward pass by hand on paper and trains its autoencoder with `loss.backward()`, but only says what automatic differentiation does). This is the likely place to explain how it works, because the VAE needs a gradient through a sampling step, and writing the sample as a deterministic function of the parameters and of independent noise (the reparameterization) is what lets the program differentiate it. Points to carry over. (1) Four ways to get a gradient: derive and code it by hand (derived in @sec-ch-meaning-as-likeness), finite differences (only the forward code, poor scaling with the number of weights, useful to check the others), symbolic differentiation (expressions can grow exponentially longer than the function), and automatic differentiation [@bishop2024deep, Section 8.2, pp. 244–245]. (2) Any program is a sequence of elementary operations with known derivatives. Running it records the sequence as a graph and the chain rule is applied operation by operation, with no formula written by anyone, exact up to rounding. (3) Two sweeps: forward mode carries the derivative with respect to one input, so $D$ inputs need $D$ passes; reverse mode, a generalization of the backpropagation of errors, records the forward pass and sweeps backwards, giving the derivative of one output with respect to every variable in one pass [@bishop2024deep, p. 249]. Training has that shape (one scalar loss, many weights), so reverse mode is what the libraries use; for the autoencoder of @sec-ch-meaning-as-likeness, 20,816 forward passes against one. (4) What it changes in practice: a new layer or loss needs only its own local derivative. Where it stops: operations with no useful derivative (a hard assignment, an argmax) need a relaxation or a gradient estimator. A natural exercise: code the backward pass of the autoencoder of @sec-ch-meaning-as-likeness by hand and check it against `loss.backward()` and against finite differences (an earlier `numpy` version of the reconstruction script of the dissolved chapter on the anatomy of embedding spaces, in the git history, did this: relative differences $2\times 10^{-16}$ and $5\times 10^{-7}$).*

<!-- salvaged from embedding-technologies-stubs/generative_spaces.qmd, section sec-denoising-diffusion-adversarial-game -->
## Denoising, Diffusion and the Adversarial Game {#sec-denoising-diffusion-adversarial-game}
*Dated history, past tense. A denoising autoencoder learns the direction towards the data; chained, it is a diffusion model. Latent diffusion works in the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder, and its conditioning typically comes from a similarity-trained encoder (CLIP), so the two kinds of space cooperate; this is where @sec-ch-meaning-across-senses meets generation. GANs replace a likelihood by a discriminator: they can sample and cannot score. One to two pages; the aim is the contrast, not a survey.*

<!-- salvaged from embedding-technologies-stubs/generative_spaces.qmd, section sec-autoregressive-masked-models-predicting -->
## Autoregressive and Masked Models: Predicting the Next Piece {#sec-autoregressive-masked-models-predicting}
*The prediction of @sec-ch-meaning-as-likeness (word2vec's softmax over the neighbour) taken to the whole sequence by the chain rule is a generative model of text; Shannon's generator and the n-gram models of @sec-ch-symbols-without-interior were already one. Its hidden vectors, not a code trained for the purpose, are the contextual vectors of @sec-ch-meaning-in-context, which is how this section hands the thread on.*

<!-- salvaged from embedding-technologies-stubs/generative_spaces.qmd, section sec-where-map-stops -->
## Where the Map Stops {#sec-where-map-stops}
*Half a page on what the two chapters leave out and why: normalising flows (invertible, so an exact way back), energy-based models, supervised and metric-learning embeddings, and the learned states of agents.*

<!-- salvaged from embedding-technologies-stubs/generative_spaces.qmd, section sec-reconciling-two-families -->
## Reconciling the Two Families {#sec-reconciling-two-families}
*What each objective pays for, in one table over the objectives of both chapters, each cell marked structural (follows from the objective) or contingent (how systems behaved at a date). A common currency, information: the InfoNCE objective as a bound on the information between two views [@oord2018representation], the reconstruction term of the evidence lower bound as a bound on the information the code keeps about the data, and the whole bound as a rate–distortion trade-off, Shannon's own. Then where the two families remain different: a bound on information says nothing about geometry, reconstruction prices every detail while contrast prices only what separates the negatives, and only the generative family has a density. The result is graded, the same family in what is kept and different in how distance is priced, and "not reducible to one objective" is an acceptable result. Every claim about bounds is to be checked against its sources before it is written.*

## Technologies That Exploit Generation {#sec-gen-technologies}
*Plan (about 1 page). Variational autoencoders, diffusion and adversarial models, autoregressive and masked language models, and latent-space steering and discovery. For each: the cost of training and of sampling, whether it parallelizes, and what the evidence at scale says of the comparison with the others; the debate between prediction in the space and scaled generative models is stated here and not settled.*

## Growing Meaning {#sec-gen-closing}
*Plan (1 page). Findings: what a latent variable model adds to a map (a new point and a score), what happens to plausibility beyond the data, and whether the sparse regions of a corpus predict later work. Achieved for the representation of meaning: meaning that can be produced, a property that the earlier list did not have and that this chapter proposes (@sec-prop-produced). Computation: the cost of sampling against the quality of what is sampled. Still out of reach: a produced object is plausible and not necessarily true, and checking it is the chapter on truth (@sec-ch-meaning-and-truth). The Epilogue collects what the tests found.*

*Sources and gaps (first pass).* Sourced in `references/`: generative grammar, the use view, Ramsey, the earlier chapter's sources on variational, diffusion and autoregressive models. Sourced in `references/` and read at the abstract only: the high-dimensional argument against interpolation and extrapolation as a distinction, the novelty of language-model text, of research ideas and of diffusion samples, the creativity surveys, the materials-embedding result, and Swanson (1990), read at the abstract and on pages 29 and 31. Not yet sourced: Boden's own account; the source on the recombination of the ideas of a prompt that the author knows; the claim that plausibility falls with distance from the data (to be measured).
